newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - No end to European M&A frenzy in sight.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - No end to European M&A frenzy in sight.

text.p: Heady levels of European mergers and acquisitions are set to continue in the first half of 1997 and perhaps beyond, with Germany and France joining Britain in the thick of the fray, corporate financiers say.
"The curious thing is we have never gone into a new year with a better order book than at the moment. A lot of deals are coming to the boil," a senior corporate financier told Reuters.
In the first nine months of 1996 cross-border mergers and acquisitions involving European Union firms totalled 1,476, a rise of 63 from 1995.
The deals were worth 39.37 billion pounds ($64.68 billion) in value, 2.66 billion pounds less than 1995, according to figures compiled by Acquistions Monthly magazine.

While next year is expected to be a good one, market players are loth to predict an increase on 1996. "We cannot conceive 1997 will be anything like 1996, which in terms of profitability has been a record year," the senior financier added.
European companies will bid for one another as well being targeted by overseas buyers, including U.S. firms. Mergers fuelled by cost savings will spur more "nil-premium" deals.

Financial services, pharmaceuticals, telecommunications, engineering, chemicals, media companies and utilities are expected to be busy and U.S. firms will again be big players in Europe, although some still feel more at home buying British where they have the advantage of a common language.

In the first nine months of the year U.S. companies accounted for 324 of those who acquired firms, followed by 183 British companies and 152 French firms. Of the sellers, 325 were German, 278 British and 187 French.
NO SIGNS OF HALTING THE FLOOD
The factors driving corporate interest in buying other firms such as low capital costs, strong cashflows and robust balance sheets in a low interest rate environment are still evident.

"If acquisition financing costs are low you can produce something that is earnings enhancing," said one financier, adding U.S. and British companies were particularly keen to utilise cheap capital for such buys.
Another force will be mounting pressure from institutional shareholders demanding that firms focus on core businesses to maximise returns, possibly leading to demergers and sales.
BRITISH MARKET REMAINS ELECTRIC

London Electricity, Yorkshire Electricity and Southern Electric are all possible targets although mergers between water companies have been largely ruled out by a government block on proposed bids for South West Water.

Hanson's energy group, due to be spun off early next year, and Imperial Tobacco, are both seen as targets along with Racal and components group T&N and there have been suggestions GEC and British Aerospace are likely to forge defence links in Europe.

Activity in the telecommunications sector is not expected to match this year's proposed British Telecom merger with MCI but mobile phone companies Vodafone and Orange are both seen as possible bid targets.
British Gas is to demerge in February and there have been rumours that a major oil firm could buy its trading arm as a vehicle to gain a large foothold in the British gas market.
Consolidation in the oil sector is expected to continue but cost-cutting takeovers among independent oil exploration and production firms are more likely than mega-mergers.
GERMAN FIRMS OPEN TO CHANGE
German companies are tipped to be busy, partly due to an opening of minds. "They are much more prepared to talk about selling and are more aggressive buyers," said one financier.

The crowded banking sector has been awash with merger talk and shares have soared since Deutsche Bank bought a stake in Bayerische Vereinsbank and Bankgesellschaft Berlin admitted to mulling a marriage with NordLB.

In telecoms talk of a possible tie-up between RWE and Veba was overtaken by the idea of a Veba merger with engineering and telecoms group Mannesmann. Thyssen's telecoms arm denied it will sell its stake in mobile phone firm E-plus to RWE or Veba. The drugs group Schering, also the focus of merger talk, has denied it is a target.
FRANCE HEATS UP
Hypermarket groups Casino and Promodes have both denied talk of a merger after Auchan's takeover last year of Docks de France. But further consolidation is expected.
In the chemicals/drugs sector restructurings could entail mergers between Synthelabo, controlled by L'Oreal , Rhone-Poulenc's Rorer subsidiary, and/or Elf-Aquitaine's Sanofi drugs unit.
Last month Club Med rallied on rumours of a bid by hotel group Accor or a foreign-based leisure group.
SWISS ON A ROLL

In Switzerland, utilities Aare-Tessin AG fuer Elektrizitaet (Atel) and EG Laufenburg are seen as candidates for mergers, alliances or takeovers. But political problems are expected if a foreign firm stages a takeover.
In engineering, there is speculation technology group Sulzer AG may break up its five major divisions, which range from orthopedics and heart pacemakers to oil well pumps.

Another spin-off candidate is shoes-to-airplane maker Oerlikon-Buehrle. In banking, CS Holding and Swiss Bank Corp are both merger possibilities while the drugs group Roche has been linked with SmithKline Beecham, Sweden's Astra and Britain's Zeneca.
BANKS AND ENGINEERING IN BELGIUM
Belgium's Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB) may merge its Tractebel and Powerfin units.

And its Banking and Finance Commission has forecast bank mergers, warning on the viability of small banks in a heavily overbanked country. Banque Bruxelles Lambert is seen as a merger or takeover candiate after a planned link with Generale Bank, Belgium's biggest bank, was shelved.

A merger in the cash-strapped Belgian steel sector had been widely expected but Belgium's largest steel-maker Cockerill Sambre last week ruled out a link with any of the two smaller steel makers in Belgium's southern Walloon region.
Privately-held Usines Gustave Boel is expected to link up with Dutch Hoogovens and Royale Belge has been dragged along in merger plans between its parent UAP and fellow French insurer Axa.
DUTCH TO LOOSEN TAKEOVER RULES
The Dutch government is due to present a new law next year limiting the power of Dutch companies to thwart hostile takeover bids and has indicated this will not lead to a frenzy of activity.

Airline KLM continues to seek a European partner while retailer and business services group Vendex is expected to invest in the supermarkets, temporary employment or office cleaning sector at home or abroad.
Bolswessanen is rumoured as under threat from Britain's Grand Met and elswhere in the food sector CSM is seen as a target, possibly of Unilever.
